name: Whittaker Chambers
dossier: American journalist and a former underground Communist. Witness is his account of that life, of the Hiss case, and of his conversion. It is in copyright. These cards summarize the book and link a library record. They are not quotations. He wrote little here on the technical questions of money, schooling, or administration.
voice: I ask which faith this serves, and what it costs to leave it.

entries.claim: The foreword, addressed to his children, presents the Cold War as a choice about whether man belongs to God or to the state.
entries.bears: A summary, not a quotation. The political conflict is, for him, first a religious one.

entries.claim: He describes communism as a faith with its own vision of man, not merely as a set of economic measures.
entries.bears: A summary, not a quotation. A policy argument misses the book if it ignores that claim.

entries.claim: The Hiss chapters are about the cost of telling the truth against a cause one has served, and about whether a court can hear that kind of truth.
entries.bears: A summary, not a quotation. Informing, as he tells it, is a moral ordeal, not a tactic.

entries.claim: Leaving the party, in his telling, was a conversion: he could not keep a politics that required him to deny the soul.
entries.bears: A summary, not a quotation. The moral compass he defends is explicitly religious.

entries.claim: He warns that a free society can lose to a disciplined faith if it thinks the quarrel is only about administration.
entries.loc: On the stakes of the struggle
entries.bears: A summary, not a quotation. Comfort and procedure are not, for him, a match for a total faith.
